theme: The potter’s house; the broken flask; Jeremiah beaten
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 18:1-20:18. Jeremiah visits a potter’s house, smashes a clay jar in front of the elders, and is beaten and put in stocks. Then he writes one of the darkest prayers in the Bible. Read the potter scene first, then chapter 20.
settingTheScene: Two sign-acts mark these chapters: the potter at his wheel (chapter 18) and the shattered flask in the Valley of Hinnom (chapter 19). The second one costs him dearly. The priest Pashhur, chief officer of the temple, has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks. When he is released, Jeremiah gives his harshest complaint to God, and the book shows us how a faithful prophet feels when faithfulness seems to ruin his life.
observation: “Behold, like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel” (18:6).
“If that nation concerning which I have spoken turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it” (18:8).
“But they say, That is in vain! We will follow our own plans” (18:12).
“So you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you” (19:10).
“Thus will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter’s vessel” (19:11).
“Then Pashhur… struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks” (20:2).
“O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed” (20:7).
“If I say, I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name, there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot” (20:9).
interpretation:
At the potter’s house, Jeremiah watches a vessel spoil in the potter’s hands, and the potter reshapes it into another. God’s lesson is about sovereignty and responsiveness. The potter has the right to shape the clay. But the passage also teaches that God responds to repentance. If a nation under judgment turns, he will relent. If a nation that was promised blessing turns to evil, he will withdraw it. The warnings and promises of the prophets are not fixed in stone but are addressed to human response. And yet the people reply, “We will follow our own plans.”

In chapter 19, Jeremiah is told to buy a finished clay jar and take the elders to the Valley of Hinnom, where children had been burned to Baal, and smash it. A clay pot that has been fired cannot be remade. The first sign-act showed that a repentant clay could be reshaped. The second shows that stubborn clay will be broken beyond repair. The message: God has been patient, but there is a point at which the vessel is hardened.

The punishment comes at once. Pashhur strikes him and puts him in the stocks overnight. Jeremiah’s reply is a blazing prophecy of exile. Then he is alone with God, and he prays one of the most honest prayers in Scripture. “You have deceived me.” He feels that God has trapped him. The word of the LORD has become a reproach and derision. Yet he cannot quit: “There is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones.” He cannot stop speaking.

He ends with trust, “the LORD is with me as a dread warrior,” and then with despair, “Cursed be the day on which I was born.” Both are in one chapter. The Bible does not tidy faith. It shows a servant of God who is faithful and in agony.
connection: Romans 9:20-21 draws on the potter and clay. Isaiah 64:8 says, “You are the potter; we are the clay.” Matthew 27:7-10 connects the potter’s field to the death of Judas, with a quotation attributed to Jeremiah. Paul speaks of treasure in jars of clay (2 Corinthians 4:7). Acts 5:40-41 shows the apostles rejoicing when beaten. Luke 24:32 describes hearts burning within as Jesus opened the Scriptures.
application:
Place one area of your life in the potter’s hands, and ask him to reshape it.

If you are discouraged in serving God, pray honestly like Jeremiah. God can handle it.

Ask for the “burning fire” of the word in your heart, and for courage to share it.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you are clay and he is the potter, and let him reshape you.
Ask him to help you when serving him hurts.
